growth_011:n1.prompt:
You are helping me run the keyword and topic research step for our SEO content engine using {{vendor}}. Before starting, ask me for: my domain/business name, the product or service we sell, 3-5 example customer pain points or use cases, and any existing target keywords or competitor sites I already know about.

Once you have this, use {{vendor}}'s web-grounded research capability (or launch a deep research run if available) to: (1) identify 15-25 candidate keyword/topic clusters relevant to my business, grouped by search intent (informational, commercial, navigational); (2) for each cluster, pull estimated relevance signals from current web results (e.g. how many strong ranking pages exist, what angles competitors use, notable subtopics) with citations back to sources; (3) flag 5-8 'quick win' topics that look lower-competition based on what you find, and 5-8 'cornerstone' topics that are broader and more competitive.

If {{vendor}} supports running code on data, use that to compute and chart a simple priority score per topic (e.g. combining estimated competition and relevance) and produce a downloadable file (CSV or spreadsheet) with columns: topic, cluster, intent, priority score, 2-3 supporting source citations, and a one-line content angle suggestion.

Done looks like: a single report or file listing prioritized topics/keywords with citations, ready to hand to a writer for drafting. Report back to me with: a summary of the top 10 recommended topics, the full file/report link or contents, and any gaps or assumptions you had to make due to missing input from me.

growth_011:n2.prompt:
You are helping me draft a piece of SEO content using {{vendor}}, our AI assistant tool, as part of our repeatable content engine. 

Before starting, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available: the target keyword/topic (and any keyword research notes I have), the target audience, desired word count, tone/voice guidelines, any brand style guide or past published posts to match, and the working title or content brief if one exists.

Once you have the inputs, do the following inside {{vendor}}:
1. Delegate the drafting task to {{vendor}}'s built-in assistant, giving it the keyword, audience, tone, and structure (intro, headers/subheads, conclusion, meta description suggestion).
2. Have the assistant produce a full draft document I can review and export (e.g. as a doc or markdown file).
3. Iteratively refine the draft with the assistant — ask it to tighten weak sections, add examples, improve headers for scannability, and ensure the target keyword and natural variations appear appropriately without stuffing.
4. If useful, have the assistant run any computation needed to produce supporting data, a simple chart, or a downloadable file to embed in the post (e.g. a comparison table or stat summary).
5. Export the final draft in a format ready for human editing (doc, markdown, or similar).

Done looks like: a complete, exported draft document with a clear title, structured headers, a suggested meta description, and any supporting assets (charts/tables) attached or linked, ready to hand off for human editing — do not publish or submit anything yourself.

Report back with: the exported draft's location/filename, a short summary of the content and structure, any supporting files produced, and any open questions or gaps you flagged for the human editor to address.

growth_011:n3.prompt:
You are helping me prepare an AI-drafted article for editorial review before publishing, as part of our SEO content loop. If you don't already have it, ask me for: the draft article (text or file/doc link), the target keyword(s) it's optimized for, our brand voice/style guide (if one exists), and any factual sources or citations used in drafting.

Once you have the draft, please:

1. Run an automated grammar and readability check, flagging typos, awkward phrasing, passive voice overuse, and sentence complexity issues.
2. Run an SEO check: confirm the target keyword(s) appear naturally in the title, headers, intro, and body; check meta title/description length; flag keyword stuffing or missing on-page elements.
3. Run a plagiarism/originality check to flag any passages that closely match existing published content.
4. Cross-check factual claims, statistics, and quotes against the sources I provide, flagging anything unsupported or unverifiable.
5. Compare tone and phrasing against our brand voice/style guide (if provided) and flag deviations.
6. Compile all findings into a single, organized editorial review checklist: grammar/readability issues, SEO issues, originality flags, factual accuracy flags, and brand-voice notes — each with the specific location in the draft and a suggested fix where possible.

Done looks like: a clear, actionable checklist and annotated draft (or comment list) that a human editor can quickly review to judge factual accuracy, brand voice fit, and overall quality — but you must not make the final call on whether the content is accurate, on-brand, or ready to publish. That judgment belongs to a human editor.

Report back with the checklist, the annotated draft (or a link to it), and a short summary of the most significant flags needing editor attention. Then stop for human sign-off — do not publish, approve, or mark the article as ready yourself.

growth_011:n4.prompt:
You are helping me publish freshly edited content to my live website using {{vendor}}, our chosen edge-platform for hosting and deployment. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) my production domain, (2) the path to the finished, human-edited content file(s) or folder (e.g., markdown/HTML output from our content loop), (3) whether the project is already connected to a Git repository in {{vendor}} or needs a folder upload instead, and (4) confirmation that you should use my already-configured {{vendor}} credentials.

Actions to take:
1. If the project has a connected Git repo, add/commit the new content in the appropriate content directory and push it so {{vendor}}'s auto-deploy-on-push picks it up. Do not modify build configuration—rely on {{vendor}}'s automatic framework detection.
2. If there is no Git repo, deploy the folder of finished files directly via {{vendor}}'s CLI or API (no repo required), keeping the resulting deployment private/preview-only until I explicitly confirm I want it public.
3. Trigger the deployment programmatically (via {{vendor}}'s CLI or API, not a web dashboard) so the process is scriptable and repeatable for future publishes.
4. Once I confirm the preview looks correct, promote/publish that deployment to production on my domain.
5. Verify the live page is reachable at the expected URL and that the new content renders correctly (title, body, no broken links/images).

Done looks like: the new content is live on my production domain via {{vendor}}, the deployment is marked production/public (not just preview), and you've confirmed the page loads correctly.

Report back with: the deployment method used (Git push vs. folder upload), the live URL(s) published, the deployment ID or reference from {{vendor}}, and confirmation of successful verification—or any errors encountered.

growth_011:n5.prompt:
You are helping me submit my site's sitemap to search engines as part of my SEO content loop. Before starting, ask me for: (1) my site's domain, (2) the full URL of my sitemap file (e.g., https://mydomain.com/sitemap.xml), and (3) whether I already have accounts set up in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools using my configured credentials.

Once you have this, do the following:
1. Confirm the sitemap URL is publicly reachable and returns valid XML (check status code and content type).
2. In Google Search Console, using my configured credentials, add/verify the property for my domain if not already verified, then submit the sitemap URL under the Sitemaps section.
3. In Bing Webmaster Tools, using my configured credentials, add/verify the same domain if not already verified, then submit the same sitemap URL.
4. If either platform reports an error (e.g., 'couldn't fetch' or 'has errors'), report the exact error message back to me along with the sitemap URL and timestamp so I can investigate.
5. If verification of the domain is required and cannot be completed automatically (e.g., requires DNS or file upload I haven't set up), describe what's needed and pause — do not attempt domain ownership verification steps that require actions outside your access.

Done looks like: both Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools show the sitemap as successfully submitted with a 'Success' or 'Pending' status (not an error state), and I have the direct dashboard URLs for both so I can monitor indexing progress myself.

Report back with: the sitemap URL submitted, confirmation status from each platform, any errors encountered, and links to both dashboards for future monitoring.

growth_011:n6.prompt:
You are helping me monitor organic traffic and content performance for our SEO & content engine using {{vendor}}, our configured product-analytics tool. Assume {{vendor}} is already connected to our site's analytics data with credentials configured.

If you don't already know them, ask me for: (1) my domain, (2) which published articles/URLs to track (or confirm you should pull all blog/content paths), and (3) the lookback window for the report (default to last 30 days if I don't specify).

Actions to take:
1. Query {{vendor}} for traffic to our published content: pageviews, unique visitors, and top landing pages, using its query/export capability (e.g. run a SQL-style query or export raw event data, or retrieve a timeseries of stats, depending on what {{vendor}} exposes).
2. Identify which content pieces are gaining or losing traffic week-over-week, and flag any pages with near-zero traffic 2+ weeks after publish (candidates for re-optimization).
3. Create or update a dashboard/saved insight in {{vendor}} showing traffic trends per article, if the tool supports programmatic dashboard creation.
4. Set up or verify an alert/subscription so a key metric (e.g. total organic traffic or a specific page's views) notifies us if it moves abnormally.
5. Summarize findings: top 3 growing pages, top 3 declining/stagnant pages, and any anomalies.

Done looks like: a working dashboard or saved query in {{vendor}} tracking our content traffic, at least one alert/subscription configured, and a written summary of current performance trends.

Report back with: the dashboard/query link or reference, the alert you configured, the traffic summary, and any pages you recommend I review or refresh for SEO.
